title: Ἀπιστία καὶ ῥήτρη
titleEn: The Swineherd’s Doubt and the Wager — Odyssey 14.321–417
part: The Swineherd’s Doubt and the Wager (14.321–417)
about: The Cretan, who is Odysseus in disguise, finishes the tale he has been telling the swineherd Eumaeus. In Thesprotia, he says, the king showed him the goods Odysseus had stored there and reported that Odysseus had gone to the oak of Zeus at Dodona to learn how to come home; but the Cretan was sent off first, on a Thesprotian ship whose crew meant to make a slave of him. Near Ithaca they bound him and went ashore for supper; the gods loosened the rope, and he swam away and hid until they gave up, and the gods then led him to the house of a man of understanding. Eumaeus answers that the story has moved him but that he cannot believe what is said of Odysseus: he is sure his lord is dead, and an Aetolian once deceived him with the same promise. The disguised Odysseus proposes a bargain, clothes and a passage to Dulichium if Eumaeus’s master comes home and a throw from a rock if he does not, and Eumaeus refuses it with bitter sarcasm. The swineherds then come in with the swine, and Eumaeus orders the best pig brought to be slaughtered for the stranger.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ Ὀδυσῆος ἐγὼ πυθόμην·
sentences.l: There of Odysseus I learned;
sentences.i: There I learned of Odysseus;
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ is ἔνθα with its final vowel elided, here ‘there’, in Thesprotia, where the previous part left the Cretan; the speaker is still Odysseus in his false character, and his speech runs on from the last part, so no opening quotation mark is set. Ὀδυσῆος is the genitive of Ὀδυσεύς with a single σ; the form with two, Ὀδυσσῆος, is the same name, the doubling being a metrical option. πυθόμην is the aorist middle of πυνθάνομαι ‘learn by inquiry, hear’, unaugmented (Attic ἐπυθόμην), and takes a genitive of the person heard about: ‘I heard of Odysseus’. The raised dot ends the unit in mid-line, and the reason follows in the next.

sentences.t:
κεῖνος γὰρ ἔφασκε
ξεινίσαι ἠδὲ φιλῆσαι ἰόντ’ ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν,
καί μοι κτήματ’ ἔδειξεν ὅσα ξυναγείρατ’ Ὀδυσσεύς,
χαλκόν τε χρυσόν τε πολύκμητόν τε σίδηρον.
sentences.l:
for that man kept saying
to have entertained and to have welcomed him, going to his fatherland,
and to me goods he showed, as many as Odysseus had gathered together,
bronze and gold and much-laboured iron.
sentences.i: for he kept saying that he had entertained and welcomed him as he was on his way to his fatherland, and he showed me the goods, as many as Odysseus had gathered together, bronze and gold and iron worked with much labour.
sentences.n: κεῖνος is ‘that man’, the king Pheidon of the last part; ἔφασκε is the iterative (-σκ-) imperfect of φημί, ‘kept saying’, and what follows is an infinitive clause, ‘that he had …’. ξεινίσαι ‘entertain as a guest’ and φιλῆσαι ‘welcome as a friend’ are aorist infinitives, and the participle ἰόντ’ (ἰόντα, elided, from εἶμι ‘go’) agrees with an unexpressed ‘him’, the object of both, Odysseus not being named in the clause. πατρίδα γαῖαν is ‘fatherland’. κτήματα is ‘goods’, and ὅσα ξυναγείρατ’ is ‘as many as he had gathered together’: ξυναγείρατο is the aorist middle of συναγείρω with the epic ξυν- for συν-. πολύκμητον is built on κάμνω ‘toil’, ‘worked with much labour’, which suits iron, a metal hard to work.

sentences.t: καί νύ κεν ἐς δεκάτην γενεὴν ἕτερόν γ’ ἔτι βόσκοι·
sentences.l: and indeed to the tenth generation another still it might feed;
sentences.i: and it could still feed another man, even to the tenth generation;
sentences.n: κεν with the optative βόσκοι makes a possibility, ‘it could feed’, and the unexpressed subject is the heap of goods just named. ἐς δεκάτην γενεήν is ‘as far as the tenth generation’, and ἕτερον is ‘another’ (man); the picture is of a store large enough to keep one man after another through ten generations. νυ, like νύ in 359, is a little particle of emphasis, ‘indeed’. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t: τόσσα οἱ ἐν μεγάροις κειμήλια κεῖτο ἄνακτος.
sentences.l: so many for him in the halls treasures lay, of the lord.
sentences.i: so many treasures lay stored up for him in the halls of the lord.
sentences.n: The genitive ἄνακτος hangs on μεγάροις, ‘in the halls of the lord’, which is the host, Pheidon, in whose house the goods are kept; οἱ is ‘for him’, Odysseus, to whom they belong. κειμήλια ‘treasures’, things laid up, is a neuter plural with the singular verb κεῖτο, the regular Greek habit. τόσσα is ‘so many’, picking up ὅσα in 323.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἐς Δωδώνην φάτο βήμεναι, ὄφρα θεοῖο
ἐκ δρυὸς ὑψικόμοιο Διὸς βουλὴν ἐπακούσαι,
ὅππως νοστήσει’ Ἰθάκης ἐς πίονα δῆμον
ἤδη δὴν ἀπεών, ἢ ἀμφαδὸν ἦε κρυφηδόν.
sentences.l:
And him to Dodona he said had gone, in order that of the god
from the high-crowned oak the plan of Zeus he might hear,
how he might return to the rich land of Ithaca,
already long away, whether openly or in secret.
sentences.i: He said that Odysseus had gone to Dodona, to hear the plan of Zeus from the high-crowned oak of the god, how he might return to the rich land of Ithaca, after being long away already, whether openly or in secret.
sentences.n: τόν is ‘him’, Odysseus, the subject of the infinitive βήμεναι, the epic form of βῆναι, so ‘said he had gone’; φάτο is the unaugmented ἔφατο. Δωδώνη (Dodona) is the oracle of Zeus in the north-west of Greece, here with an oak: the god’s plan is heard ‘from the high-crowned oak’, ὑψικόμοιο being ‘high-crowned’ as in the table’s ὑψικόμοισι δρυσί. ὄφρα with the optative ἐπακούσαι (aorist, ‘might hear’) states the purpose, and νοστήσει’ is the optative νοστήσειε, elided, in an indirect question, ‘how he might come home’. δῆμος is ‘land’ and πίων, ‘fat’ of flocks, is ‘rich’ of a country. ἀπεών is the Ionic participle of ἄπειμι ‘be away’, and ἀμφαδόν and κρυφηδόν are adverbs, ‘openly’ and ‘secretly’; ἦε is ἤ ‘or’.

sentences.t:
ὤμοσε δὲ πρὸς ἔμ’ αὐτόν, ἀποσπένδων ἐνὶ οἴκῳ,
νῆα κατειρύσθαι καὶ ἐπαρτέας ἔμμεν ἑταίρους,
οἳ δή μιν πέμψουσι φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.l:
And he swore, to me myself, pouring a libation in his house,
that a ship had been drawn down and that ready were companions
who indeed would send him to his dear fatherland.
sentences.i: And in his house, pouring a libation, he swore to me in person that a ship had been drawn down and that companions were ready who were to send Odysseus on to his dear fatherland.
sentences.n: The subject of ὤμοσε ‘swore’ is still the king; πρὸς ἔμ’ αὐτόν is ‘to me myself’, in my presence, and ἀποσπένδων is ‘pouring a libation’, the pouring that went with an oath. The oath is reported in an infinitive clause: κατειρύσθαι is the perfect passive infinitive of κατερύω ‘draw down’, a ship ‘has been drawn down’ to the water, that is launched, and ἔμμεν is ἔμμεναι ‘be’ (Attic εἶναι), with ἐπαρτέας ‘ready’. The relative clause keeps the future of the original promise, πέμψουσι ‘will send’, and μιν is Odysseus; φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν is ‘to his dear fatherland’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἐμὲ πρὶν ἀπέπεμψε·
sentences.l: But me before that he sent away;
sentences.i: But he sent me away before that;
sentences.n: The subject of ἀπέπεμψε (aorist of ἀποπέμπω ‘send away’) is the king, and ἐμέ is stressed: me, and not Odysseus, was sent first. πρίν is here an adverb, ‘before, earlier’, the king sent the Cretan off before the sailing he had promised Odysseus. The unit is cut at the raised dot in mid-line.

sentences.t:
τύχησε γὰρ ἐρχομένη νηῦς
ἀνδρῶν Θεσπρωτῶν ἐς Δουλίχιον πολύπυρον.
sentences.l:
for happened going a ship
of Thesprotian men to Dulichium, rich in wheat.
sentences.i: for a ship of Thesprotian men happened to be on its way to Dulichium, rich in wheat.
sentences.n: τύχησε is the aorist of τυγχάνω ‘happen’, and with the participle ἐρχομένη it is ‘happened to be going’. ἀνδρῶν Θεσπρωτῶν is ‘of Thesprotian men’ and depends on νηῦς. Δουλίχιον is the place-name Dulichium; πολύπυρον, ‘rich in wheat’, is built on πολύς and πυρός ‘wheat’ and is the epithet that goes with it here, as πολύχρυσος ‘rich in gold’ goes with Mycenae.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ὅ γέ μ’ ἠνώγει πέμψαι βασιλῆϊ Ἀκάστῳ
ἐνδυκέως·
sentences.l:
Then he, for his part, bade (them) send me to king Acastus
kindly;
sentences.i: Then he told them to send me kindly to King Acastus;
sentences.n: ἠνώγει is the past tense of ἄνωγα (pluperfect in form, imperfect in sense), ‘bade’, and the subject is ὅ γε, ‘he’, the king; those he bade, the ship’s crew, are not named, and πέμψαι is the aorist infinitive ‘to send’, with με as its object, ‘to send me’. βασιλῆϊ is the Ionic dative of βασιλεύς; Acastus, here called king and nothing more, is not described in these lines. ἐνδυκέως is ‘kindly’ in the house style: it also means ‘with careful attention’. The unit is cut at the raised dot after it.

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δὲ κακὴ φρεσὶν ἥνδανε βουλὴ
ἀμφ’ ἐμοί, ὄφρ’ ἔτι πάγχυ δύης ἐπὶ πῆμα γενοίμην.
sentences.l:
but to them an evil plan in their minds was pleasing
about me, so that still utterly to a woe of misery I might come.
sentences.i: but they were pleased in their minds with an evil plan about me, so that I might still come, utterly, to a woe of misery.
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is ‘to them’, the sailors, set against the king. ἥνδανε is the imperfect of ἁνδάνω ‘please’ (with augment, Attic ἐήνδανε), ‘was pleasing’, and ἀμφ’ ἐμοί is ‘about me’: ἀμφί with the dative means ‘concerning’. ὄφρα with the optative γενοίμην gives the purpose, ‘so that I might come to’. δύη is ‘misery’ and πῆμα ‘woe’, so δύης ἐπὶ πῆμα is a woe that consists in misery; ἔτι πάγχυ is ‘still, altogether’. The phrase is compressed, and the sense given is that they wanted to push him to the extreme of suffering.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε γαίης πολλὸν ἀπέπλω ποντοπόρος νηῦς,
αὐτίκα δούλιον ἦμαρ ἐμοὶ περιμηχανόωντο.
sentences.l:
But when from land far off sailed the sea-crossing ship,
at once the day of slavery for me they devised thoroughly.
sentences.i: But when the sea-crossing ship had sailed far from land, at once they set about devising a day of slavery for me.
sentences.n: γαίης is a genitive of separation, ‘from land’, with πολλόν ‘far’, and ἀπέπλω is ‘sailed away’ (ἀποπλέω). ποντοπόρος νηῦς is ‘sea-crossing ship’, the house rendering. δούλιον ἦμαρ is ‘the day of slavery’: ἦμαρ is ‘day’ standing for the state that day brings, as in νόστιμον ἦμαρ ‘the homecoming day’ (1.9). περιμηχανόωντο is the imperfect of περιμηχανάομαι ‘devise thoroughly’ with its middle ending uncontracted (-όωντο for -ῶντο); μηχανάομαι is ‘devise’, the family of πολυμήχανος.

sentences.t:
ἐκ μέν με χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε εἵματ’ ἔδυσαν,
ἀμφὶ δέ μοι ῥάκος ἄλλο κακὸν βάλον ἠδὲ χιτῶνα,
ῥωγαλέα, τὰ καὶ αὐτὸς ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ὅρηαι·
sentences.i: They stripped me of my cloak and tunic, my clothes, and threw another vile rag about me, and a tunic, torn things, which you can see for yourself with your own eyes;
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἔδυσαν is tmesis for ἐξέδυσαν, a causative aorist of δύω ‘strip’, and με is the person, the clothes the thing: ‘stripped me of cloak and tunic, clothes’, the stock phrase χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε εἵματα. ἀμφὶ … βάλον is tmesis for ἀμφέβαλον ‘threw about’. ῥάκος ἄλλο κακόν is ‘another, an evil rag’, ‘another’ meaning a different one, and a poor one; ῥωγαλέα ‘torn’ is neuter plural and agrees with both rag and tunic. ὅρηαι is the epic second person of ὁράω, ‘you see’; its ending looks like that of a middle subjunctive, but the sense is plain present. The speaker points to the clothes he is wearing as he speaks.

sentences.t: ἑσπέριοι δ’ Ἰθάκης εὐδειέλου ἔργ’ ἀφίκοντο.
sentences.l: And in the evening the works of clear-seen Ithaca they reached.
sentences.i: And toward evening they reached the cultivated land of clear-seen Ithaca.
sentences.n: ἑσπέριοι is a plural adjective where English has an adverb, ‘at evening’; the Greek puts the people in the evening, not the action. ἔργα is ‘works’, here the lands that men work, fields and farms, and ἀφίκοντο (ἀφικνέομαι) takes it as accusative, ‘arrived at’. εὐδείελος is ‘clear-seen’, the house rendering; the ancient explanations conflict, ‘visible’ from δῆλος or ‘of the evening’ from δείελος, and the house keeps the literal ‘clear-seen’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἐμὲ μὲν κατέδησαν ἐϋσσέλμῳ ἐνὶ νηῒ
ὅπλῳ ἐϋστρεφέϊ στερεῶς, αὐτοὶ δ’ ἀποβάντες
ἐσσυμένως παρὰ θῖνα θαλάσσης δόρπον ἕλοντο.
sentences.l:
There me, indeed, they bound down in the well-benched ship
with a well-twisted rope, firmly, and they themselves, having gone ashore,
hastily along the shore of the sea took supper.
sentences.i: There they bound me down firmly in the well-benched ship with a well-twisted rope, and they themselves went ashore and hastily took their supper along the shore of the sea.
sentences.n: κατέδησαν is the aorist of καταδέω ‘bind down, fast’; ἐϋσσέλμῳ is ‘well-benched’ (the σέλμα is a ship’s plank or bench), the house rendering. ὅπλῳ ἐϋστρεφέϊ is ‘with a well-twisted rope’: ὅπλον is any piece of tackle, ‘gear’ in the plural, and a rope here. ἀποβάντες is ‘having stepped off’, and αὐτοί ‘they themselves’ sets them against their prisoner. ἐσσυμένως is an adverb from the participle of σεύομαι ‘rush’, ‘hastily’. δόρπον ἕλοντο is ‘took supper’ (αἱρέω, middle), and παρὰ θῖνα θαλάσσης ‘along the shore of the sea’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ δεσμὸν μὲν ἀνέγναμψαν θεοὶ αὐτοὶ
ῥηϊδίως·
sentences.l:
But for me the bond, indeed, unbent the gods themselves
easily;
sentences.i: But the gods themselves loosened the bond for me, easily;
sentences.n: ἀνέγναμψαν is the aorist of ἀναγνάμπτω ‘bend back’, so ‘unbent’, undid. ἐμοί is a dative of advantage, ‘for me’, and θεοὶ αὐτοί is ‘the gods themselves’, the Cretan’s claim that the gods themselves freed him. ῥηϊδίως is Ionic ‘easily’ (Attic ῥᾳδίως), and returns at 358. The raised dot falls in mid-line, so the unit ends after it.

sentences.t:
κεφαλῇ δὲ κατὰ ῥάκος ἀμφικαλύψας,
ξεστὸν ἐφόλκαιον καταβὰς ἐπέλασσα θαλάσσῃ
στῆθος, ἔπειτα δὲ χερσὶ διήρεσσ’ ἀμφοτέρῃσι
νηχόμενος, μάλα δ’ ὦκα θύρηθ’ ἔα ἀμφὶς ἐκείνων.
sentences.l:
and on my head, down, the rag having enfolded,
the polished epholkaion having gone down, I brought near to the sea
my breast, and then with both hands I rowed through
swimming, and very quickly outside I was, apart from them.
sentences.i: I enfolded the rag down about my head, went down the polished epholkaion, brought my chest to the sea, and then rowed my way through with both hands, swimming, and very quickly I was out of their reach, apart from them.
sentences.n: ἐφόλκαιον is a word of unknown meaning. From the line it is something smooth (ξεστόν, ‘polished’) that a man can go down to reach the water. ‘Rudder’, ‘ladder’ and ‘gangway’ have all been guessed, and the English leaves it untranslated. κεφαλῇ … κατὰ … ἀμφικαλύψας is tmesis with a double preverb, ‘enfolding the rag down about my head’; ἀμφικαλύπτω is ‘enfold’. καταβάς is ‘having gone down’, ἐπέλασσα ‘I brought near’ (πελάζω), and διήρεσσ’ is ‘I rowed through’, as the table has it; νηχόμενος is ‘swimming’. θύρηθ’ is an elided adverb ‘outside, out of doors’, ending in -θι (place where) or -θε, and ἔα is ‘I was’, the epic first person imperfect of εἰμί; ἀμφίς is ‘apart’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἀναβάς, ὅθι τε δρίος ἦν πολυανθέος ὕλης,
κείμην πεπτηώς.
sentences.l:
There having come up, where there was a thicket of much-flowering wood,
I lay, crouching.
sentences.i: There I climbed up to where there was a thicket of richly flowering woodland, and lay crouching.
sentences.n: ἀναβάς is ‘having come up’, out of the sea. ὅθι τε is ‘where’, with epic τε; δρίος is a thicket or copse, and πολυανθέος, genitive of πολυανθής ‘with many flowers’, agrees with ὕλης ‘wood’. κείμην is the imperfect of κεῖμαι ‘lie’, and πεπτηώς is the perfect participle of πτήσσω ‘cower, crouch’, in its epic form (-ηώς for -ώς).

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ μεγάλα στενάχοντες
φοίτων·
sentences.l:
and they, greatly groaning,
went to and fro;
sentences.i: but they went to and fro, groaning heavily;
sentences.n: οἱ δέ is ‘and they’, the crew: οἱ is the old demonstrative pronoun, not the article of later Greek. μεγάλα is a neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘greatly, heavily’, and στενάχοντες is ‘groaning’ (στενάχω, related to στένω). φοίτων is the imperfect of φοιτάω ‘go to and fro’, the repeated coming and going of a search. The dot after it ends the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐ γάρ σφιν ἐφαίνετο κέρδιον εἶναι
μαίεσθαι προτέρω, τοὶ μὲν πάλιν αὖτις ἔβαινον
νηὸς ἔπι γλαφυρῆς·
sentences.i: but since it did not seem to them better to search any farther, they went back again to the hollow ship;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὐ γάρ is ‘but since … not’: ἀλλά gives the contrast with the search, and γάρ the reason. σφιν is σφισιν ‘to them’; ἐφαίνετο κέρδιον εἶναι is ‘it appeared better’ (κέρδιον is the comparative of κέρδος ‘gain’, house ‘better’), and μαίεσθαι is the infinitive of μαίομαι ‘seek, search’. προτέρω is ‘farther on’. τοί is οἱ ‘they’, in its epic form; πάλιν αὖτις is two words for ‘back again’. νηὸς ἔπι has the accent drawn back because the preposition ἐπί follows its noun, ‘onto the ship’; γλαφυρῆς is ‘hollow’, the house rendering.

sentences.t:
ἐμὲ δ’ ἔκρυψαν θεοὶ αὐτοὶ
ῥηϊδίως, καί με σταθμῷ ἐπέλασσαν ἄγοντες
ἀνδρὸς ἐπισταμένου·
sentences.i: but the gods themselves hid me, easily, and led me close to the steading of a man of understanding;
sentences.n: ἔκρυψαν is the aorist of κρύπτω ‘hide’, with θεοὶ αὐτοί ‘the gods themselves’ and ῥηϊδίως ‘easily’ repeating 348–349. σταθμῷ is the dative after ἐπέλασσαν ‘brought near’, and σταθμός is a steading, a place where stock stand (the word is from the root of ἵστημι ‘stand’), so a farmstead. ἐπισταμένου is the participle of ἐπίσταμαι ‘know, understand’ with no object given: a man who understands, who knows what he is about. The story has been brought round to the present: the steading is the one where the Cretan now sits, and the man of understanding is the host he is speaking to. ἄγοντες is ‘leading’. The raised dot ends the unit mid-line.

sentences.t: ἔτι γάρ νύ μοι αἶσα βιῶναι.
sentences.l: for still, then, for me a portion (was) to live.”
sentences.i: for it was still my lot to live.”
sentences.n: ἔτι γάρ νυ is ‘for still, then’, νυ again a little particle of emphasis, and no verb is written: ‘was’ is understood. αἶσα is ‘portion’, the share of life allotted to a man, and βιῶναι is the aorist infinitive of βιόω ‘live’, ‘to live on, to survive’. The Cretan’s tale ends here; the speech was opened at 14.191, two parts back, and is closed with the quotation mark.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα·
sentences.l: Him, answering, you addressed, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.i: In answer you said to him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.n: This line has the same English as where it first occurs. τόν is the pronoun ‘him’; ἀπαμειβόμενος is the participle of ἀπαμείβομαι ‘answer’. προσέφης is the second person of the aorist προσέφη ‘addressed’: the poet speaks to Eumaeus as ‘you’, where the formula elsewhere has ‘he’ (compare 390), and Εὔμαιε συβῶτα are the vocatives of Εὔμαιος and συβώτης ‘swineherd’.

sentences.t:
ἆ δειλὲ ξείνων, ἦ μοι μάλα θυμὸν ὄρινας
ταῦτα ἕκαστα λέγων, ὅσα δὴ πάθες ἠδ’ ὅσ’ ἀλήθης.
sentences.l:
“Oh, miserable one among strangers, truly my heart you have greatly stirred,
these things, each thing, telling, as many as you suffered and as many as you wandered.
sentences.i: “Oh, miserable man among strangers, you have truly stirred my heart deeply, telling each of these things, all that you suffered and all your wanderings.
sentences.n: ἆ δειλέ is ‘oh, miserable one’, the house rendering of δειλός; ξείνων is a partitive genitive plural, ‘among strangers’. ἦ is ‘truly’; μοι is the dative of the person affected, ‘for me’, and ὄρινας is the aorist of ὀρίνω ‘stir, rouse’, with θυμόν ‘heart’. ἕκαστα is ‘each thing’, so ταῦτα ἕκαστα is ‘each of these things’. πάθες is the unaugmented aorist of πάσχω ‘suffer’, and ἀλήθης the unaugmented aorist passive of ἀλάομαι ‘wander’, both second person; ὅσ’ ἀλήθης is ‘as many as you wandered’, the extent of the wandering.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τά γ’ οὐ κατὰ κόσμον ὀΐομαι, οὐδέ με πείσεις
εἰπὼν ἀμφ’ Ὀδυσῆϊ·
sentences.l:
But these things not in due order I think, and not me will you persuade
speaking about Odysseus;
sentences.i: But I think those things are not as they should be, and you will not persuade me by speaking about Odysseus;
sentences.n: τά γ’ is ‘those things’ (γε stresses them), the stranger’s story of Odysseus. οὐ κατὰ κόσμον is ‘not in due order’, not as things ought to be, said here of the stranger’s story. ὀΐομαι is ‘I think, suppose’, and πείσεις the future of πείθω ‘persuade’, with εἰπών ‘by saying’. ἀμφ’ Ὀδυσῆϊ is ‘about Odysseus’: ἀμφί with the dative is Homer’s way of saying ‘concerning’, where Attic uses περί with the genitive. The raised dot ends the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t:
τί σε χρὴ τοῖον ἐόντα
μαψιδίως ψεύδεσθαι;
sentences.l:
why you is it needful, being such a one,
without cause to lie?
sentences.i: Why must a man like you lie without cause?
sentences.n: χρή takes the accusative of the person, σε, and an infinitive: ‘why must you’. τοῖον ἐόντα is ‘being such (as you are)’, pointing at the stranger as he sits there in his rags. μαψιδίως is ‘without cause’, as at 7.309, where the same adverb stands with an infinitive of anger, and ψεύδεσθαι is ‘to lie’. The Greek question mark ends the unit.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δ’ εὖ οἶδα καὶ αὐτὸς
νόστον ἐμοῖο ἄνακτος, ὅ τ’ ἤχθετο πᾶσι θεοῖσι
πάγχυ μάλ’, ὅττι μιν οὔ τι μετὰ Τρώεσσι δάμασσαν
ἠὲ φίλων ἐν χερσίν, ἐπεὶ πόλεμον τολύπευσε.
sentences.l:
But I well know, even myself,
the homecoming of my lord, that he was hateful to all the gods
utterly, very much, because not at all among the Trojans they subdued him
or in the arms of his friends, after he had wound up the war.
sentences.i: But I myself know well of my lord’s homecoming, that he was utterly hateful to all the gods, because they did not overcome him among the Trojans or in the arms of his friends, once he had wound up the war.
sentences.n: εὖ οἶδα καὶ αὐτός is ‘I know well myself’. νόστον ἐμοῖο ἄνακτος is ‘the homecoming of my lord’, ἐμοῖο being the epic genitive of ἐμός; νόστον is the object of οἶδα, and ὅ τ’ (ὅ τε) works as ‘that’ and explains it. ἤχθετο is ‘was hateful’ (ἔχθομαι) with πᾶσι θεοῖσι ‘to all the gods’; πάγχυ μάλα are two intensifiers, ‘utterly’. ὅττι is ὅτι ‘because’; δάμασσαν is the unaugmented aorist of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, and φίλων ἐν χερσίν is ‘in the arms of friends’. τολύπευσε is from τολύπη ‘ball of wool’: ‘wound up’ the war, wound it to its end. The reasoning is Eumaeus’s own, and δάμασσαν has no stated subject; the next lines say what he thinks a death at Troy would have brought, a mound and fame.

sentences.t:
τῷ κέν οἱ τύμβον μὲν ἐποίησαν Παναχαιοί,
ἠδέ κε καὶ ᾧ παιδὶ μέγα κλέος ἤρατ’ ὀπίσσω
νῦν δέ μιν ἀκλειῶς ἅρπυιαι ἀνηρείψαντο.
sentences.l:
Then for him a mound the Achaeans all together would have made,
and for his own son too great fame he would have won hereafter.
But now, without fame, the Harpies have snatched him away.
sentences.i: Then all the Achaeans would have raised a mound over him, and he would have won great fame for his son as well, in time to come. But as it is, the Harpies have carried him off without fame.
sentences.n: These three lines have, line by line, the English they have where they stand earlier in the poem (1.239–241). τῷ is ‘in that case, then’. κέν with the aorists ἐποίησαν and ἤρατ’ (ἤρατο, aorist middle of ἄρνυμαι ‘win’) makes a past that did not happen, ‘would have made, would have won’. τύμβος is a burial mound; Παναχαιοί is ‘the Achaeans all together’, and ᾧ παιδί ‘his own son’, ὅς as the possessive. The source prints no stop at the end of 370, so the unit runs on through νῦν δέ, ‘but as things are’, against the case that did not happen. ἀκλειῶς is ‘without fame’. ἅρπυιαι is a common noun, ‘snatchers’, the storm-winds, from the root of ἁρπάζω ‘snatch’; ἀνηρείψαντο is the aorist middle of ἀνερείπομαι ‘snatch up’.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ παρ’ ὕεσσιν ἀπότροπος·
sentences.l: But I beside the swine, turned away;
sentences.i: But I am out of the way, beside the swine;
sentences.n: There is no verb: ‘I am’ is understood. αὐτάρ is ‘but’, παρά with the dative ‘beside’, and ὕεσσι is the epic dative plural of ὗς ‘swine’. ἀπότροπος is ‘turned away’, from ἀποτρέπω, so remote, out of the way; Eumaeus lives apart, and the next lines explain what that costs him in news. The unit ends at the raised dot, mid-line.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ πόλινδε
ἔρχομαι, εἰ μή πού τι περίφρων Πηνελόπεια
ἐλθέμεν ὀτρύνῃσιν, ὅτ’ ἀγγελίη ποθὲν ἔλθῃ.
sentences.l:
nor to the town
do I go, unless, perhaps, circumspect Penelope
urges (me) to come, when a message from somewhere comes.
sentences.i: and I do not go to the town unless perhaps circumspect Penelope urges me to come, when some news arrives from somewhere.
sentences.n: πόλινδε is ‘to the town’ (-δε marks motion towards). εἰ μή is ‘unless’, and ὀτρύνῃσιν is the subjunctive (the ending -σιν is epic) of ὀτρύνω ‘urge’: εἰ with the subjunctive and no κεν is common in Homer. πού τι is ‘perhaps in some way’. περίφρων Πηνελόπεια is ‘circumspect Penelope’, the house rendering. ἐλθέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἔρχομαι, and ὅτ’ ἀγγελίη ποθὲν ἔλθῃ ‘when a message comes from somewhere’ is another subjunctive clause (ὅτε without ἄν); the object of ‘urges’, ‘me’, is understood.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οἱ μὲν τὰ ἕκαστα παρήμενοι ἐξερέουσιν,
ἠμὲν οἳ ἄχνυνται δὴν οἰχομένοιο ἄνακτος,
ἠδ’ οἳ χαίρουσιν βίοτον νήποινον ἔδοντες·
sentences.i: But they sit by and ask about every detail, both those who grieve for their lord, long gone, and those who are glad to devour his living and pay nothing for it;
sentences.n: οἱ μέν is ‘they’, the people in the town; its contrast comes at 378, ἀλλ’ ἐμοί, and the two groups ἠμέν … ἠδέ ‘both … and’ stand in apposition to οἱ. τὰ ἕκαστα is ‘each of the matters’, and παρήμενοι ‘sitting beside’, as people sit by a newcomer to hear his news. ἐξερέουσιν is an uncontracted form (-έουσι, for -οῦσι) of ἐξερέω ‘ask out, question closely’; it could be read as present or future, and the sense is a habit. ἄχνυνται is ‘grieve’, and δὴν οἰχομένοιο ἄνακτος is ‘for the lord long gone’ (οἴχομαι ‘be gone’). βίοτον νήποινον is ‘livelihood unpunished’: νήποινος is from ποινή ‘penalty, price’, so ‘unpaid for’, and ἔδοντες is ‘eating’, in the house ‘devour’. The suitors are the second group. The raised dot ends the unit.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐμοὶ οὐ φίλον ἐστὶ μεταλλῆσαι καὶ ἐρέσθαι,
ἐξ οὗ δή μ’ Αἰτωλὸς ἀνὴρ ἐξήπαφε μύθῳ,
ὅς ῥ’ ἄνδρα κτείνας, πολλὴν ἐπὶ γαῖαν ἀληθείς,
ἦλθεν ἐμὰ πρὸς δώματ’·
sentences.l:
But to me it is not dear to inquire and to ask,
ever since an Aetolian man deceived me with a tale,
who, a man having killed, over much land having wandered,
came to my halls;
sentences.i: But I have no wish to inquire or to ask, not since an Aetolian deceived me with a tale: a man who had killed someone and wandered over much land, and who came to my halls;
sentences.n: οὐ φίλον ἐστί is ‘it is not dear to me’, with the infinitives μεταλλῆσαι ‘inquire’ and ἐρέσθαι ‘ask’. ἐξ οὗ is ‘ever since’, literally ‘from which (time)’; ἐξήπαφε is the aorist of ἐξαπαφίσκω ‘deceive’, and μύθῳ ‘with a tale’. Αἰτωλός is ‘Aetolian’, from Aetolia on the north side of the Gulf of Corinth. ὅς ῥ’ is ‘who’ with a particle; ἄνδρα κτείνας is ‘having killed a man’, which explains why he was wandering: a man who had killed was an exile who needed a house to take him in. ἀληθείς is the aorist passive participle of ἀλάομαι, ‘having wandered’; ἐμὰ δώματα is ‘my halls’, δώματα being ‘halls’ in the house style even of Eumaeus’s modest steading. The raised dot ends the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t: ἐγὼ δέ μιν ἀμφαγάπαζον.
sentences.l: and I him warmly welcomed.
sentences.i: and I welcomed him warmly.
sentences.n: ἀμφαγάπαζον is the imperfect of ἀμφαγαπάζω ‘welcome warmly’: ἀγαπάζω is ‘welcome with affection’, and ἀμφί, ‘on both sides, all round’, makes it fuller. The imperfect gives ‘I went on welcoming him’. The sentence is short against the long one before it.

sentences.t:
φῆ δέ μιν ἐν Κρήτεσσι παρ’ Ἰδομενῆϊ ἰδέσθαι
νῆας ἀκειόμενον, τάς οἱ ξυνέαξαν ἄελλαι·
sentences.l:
And he said he had seen him among the Cretans, beside Idomeneus,
mending ships, which for him had shattered blasts;
sentences.i: He said that he had seen Odysseus among the Cretans, with Idomeneus, repairing his ships, which the storms had shattered for him;
sentences.n: φῆ is the unaugmented ἔφη ‘he said’, the subject being the Aetolian, and μιν is Odysseus, the object of the infinitive ἰδέσθαι ‘to have seen’ (its subject is the Aetolian again), with ἀκειόμενον ‘mending’ agreeing with μιν; ἐν Κρήτεσσι is ‘among the Cretans’, παρ’ Ἰδομενῆϊ ‘beside Idomeneus’, the Cretan leader. ἀκειόμενον is the present participle of ἀκέομαι ‘mend, heal’, here of repairing ships. τάς οἱ ξυνέαξαν ἄελλαι is ‘which blasts had broken for him’: ξυνέαξαν is the aorist of συνάγνυμι ‘break to pieces’, οἱ is ‘for him’, and ἄελλαι are ‘blasts’ of wind, gales. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
καὶ φάτ’ ἐλεύσεσθαι ἢ ἐς θέρος ἢ ἐς ὀπώρην,
πολλὰ χρήματ’ ἄγοντα, σὺν ἀντιθέοις ἑτάροισι.
sentences.l:
and he said he would come either by summer or by late summer,
bringing many goods, with godlike companions.
sentences.i: and he said that he would come either by summer or by late summer, bringing many goods, with his godlike companions.
sentences.n: φάτ’ is ἔφατο ‘he said’ (imperfect middle, unaugmented), with ἐλεύσεσθαι, the future infinitive of ἔρχομαι, ‘would come’. ἐς θέρος is ‘by summer’: ἐς with a time means ‘by, up to’. ὀπώρη is the late-summer season, when fruit ripens, not autumn in the English sense. ἄγοντα is the accusative participle agreeing with the unexpressed ‘him’, ‘bringing’, and πολλὰ χρήματα is ‘many goods’. ἀντιθέοις is ‘godlike’, the house rendering, a stock word that says nothing here about their character.

sentences.t:
καὶ σύ, γέρον πολυπενθές, ἐπεί σέ μοι ἤγαγε δαίμων,
μήτε τί μοι ψεύδεσσι χαρίζεο μήτε τι θέλγε·
sentences.l:
And you, old man of many griefs, since a power has led you to me,
neither in any way me with lies gratify, nor in any way enchant;
sentences.i: And you, old man of many griefs, since some power has brought you to me, do not gratify me with lies in any way, and do not enchant me;
sentences.n: καὶ σύ is ‘you too’, as the Aetolian did; γέρον is a vocative, and πολυπενθές the vocative of πολυπενθής ‘of many griefs’, from πένθος ‘grief, mourning’. δαίμων is ‘a power’, some unnamed divine agency, the house rendering, and ἤγαγε the aorist of ἄγω. The two commands are imperatives with μήτε … μήτε ‘neither … nor’: χαρίζεο is the middle of χαρίζομαι ‘gratify, do a favour to’, with the dative μοι and ψεύδεσσι ‘with lies’, and θέλγε is the imperative of θέλγω ‘enchant’, with ‘me’ understood. τι is an adverb, ‘at all’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ τοὔνεκ’ ἐγώ σ’ αἰδέσσομαι οὐδὲ φιλήσω,
ἀλλὰ Δία ξένιον δείσας αὐτόν τ’ ἐλεαίρων.
sentences.l:
For not on that account will I revere you or welcome you,
but Zeus, the guest-god, having feared, and you yourself pitying.”
sentences.i: For I will not show you respect or welcome you on that account, but out of fear of Zeus, the god of guests, and pity for you yourself.”
sentences.n: τοὔνεκα is τοῦ ἕνεκα ‘on that account’, with the final vowel elided, and ‘that’ is the flattery. αἰδέσσομαι is the future of αἰδέομαι ‘revere, treat with respect’ (αἰδώς is the awe owed to a guest or suppliant), and φιλήσω is ‘I shall welcome’, the host’s verb of 322. ξένιον is the adjective ξένιος ‘of guests’, here with Δία ‘Zeus’, the god who guards guests; δείσας is the aorist participle of δείδω ‘fear’, and αὐτόν is ‘you yourself’. ἐλεαίρων is ‘pitying’. Eumaeus ends by saying he will be kind for the right reasons, which are not belief. The speech ends here, and the quotation mark closes.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς
ἦ μάλα τίς τοι θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἄπιστος,
οἷόν σ’ οὐδ’ ὀμόσας περ ἐπήγαγον οὐδέ σε πείθω.
sentences.l:
Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
“Truly, what a heart you have in your breast, unbelieving,
such that you not even, though I swore, did I bring round, nor do I persuade you.
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him: “What an unbelieving heart you have in your breast! Even when I swore an oath I did not win you over, and I do not persuade you.
sentences.n: The reply-formula, ‘answering, addressed’, has the same English as where it first occurs. After the ‘you’ of 360 the poet is back to the third person. The source prints no stop at the end of 390, so the formula and the speech’s first sentence are one unit here, as at 14.191. ἦ μάλα is ‘truly’, and τίς with the noun is exclamatory, ‘what a heart’; τοι is σοι, a dative of possession, and ἄπιστος is ‘unbelieving’. οἷον (neuter of οἷος ‘of such a kind’) is an adverb, ‘such that’. ὀμόσας is the aorist participle of ὄμνυμι ‘swear’, with περ ‘even though’; ἐπήγαγον is the aorist of ἐπάγω ‘bring over’; οὐδέ σε πείθω is the present tense of an attempt that does not succeed.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν ῥήτρην ποιησόμεθ’·
sentences.l: But come now, an agreement let us make;
sentences.i: But come now, let us make an agreement;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν is ‘but come now’, the house phrase. ποιησόμεθ’ is a short-vowel aorist subjunctive middle of ποιέω, ‘let us make’, spelled like the future, which would give much the same sense. ῥήτρη is ‘agreement’, a spoken pledge, from the root of ἐρῶ ‘say’ that gives ῥῆμα ‘word’; it names a bargain with terms and penalties, which the next lines spell out. The unit ends at the raised dot in mid-line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὄπισθε
μάρτυροι ἀμφοτέροισι θεοί, τοὶ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσιν.
sentences.l:
and hereafter
witnesses for us both (be) the gods, who hold Olympus.
sentences.i: and hereafter let the gods who hold Olympus be witnesses for us both.
sentences.n: ὄπισθε is ‘behind’, of time ‘afterwards, in time to come’. There is no verb: μάρτυροι, nominative plural of μάρτυς ‘witness’, stands with ‘be’ or ‘let them be’ understood. ἀμφοτέροισι is the dative ‘for both of us’, and τοί is οἱ, ‘who’; Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσιν is ‘hold Olympus’, the gods being those who have Olympus as their dwelling.

sentences.t:
εἰ μέν κεν νοστήσῃ ἄναξ τεὸς ἐς τόδε δῶμα,
ἕσσας με χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε εἵματα πέμψαι
Δουλίχιόνδ’ ἰέναι, ὅθι μοι φίλον ἔπλετο θυμῷ·
sentences.i: If your lord does come home to this house, clothe me in a cloak and a tunic as clothes, and send me to go to Dulichium, where it has grown dear to my heart;
sentences.n: εἰ μέν κεν νοστήσῃ is ‘if indeed he should come home’: εἰ with κεν and a subjunctive. ἄναξ τεός is ‘your lord’, τεός being the epic σός. ἕσσας is the aorist participle of ἕννυμι ‘clothe’ with two accusatives, me and the garments, the stock phrase χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε εἵματα ‘cloak and tunic, clothes’; the stranger described (341–343) the rags he wears now. πέμψαι has the force of a command, ‘send me’; the form is the aorist infinitive or the middle imperative, and both read the same. ἰέναι ‘to go’ completes it. Δουλίχιόνδ’ is ‘to Dulichium’ (-δε), and ὅθι μοι φίλον ἔπλετο θυμῷ is ‘where it has become dear to me in my heart’, ἔπλετο being the aorist of πέλομαι. The raised dot ends the unit.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κε μὴ ἔλθῃσιν ἄναξ τεὸς ὡς ἀγορεύω,
δμῶας ἐπισσεύας βαλέειν μεγάλης κατὰ πέτρης,
ὄφρα καὶ ἄλλος πτωχὸς ἀλεύεται ἠπεροπεύειν.
sentences.l:
But if your lord should not come as I say,
having set your servants on, throw (me) down from a great rock,
so that another beggar also may shun deceiving.”
sentences.i: But if your lord does not come as I say, set your servants on me and have them throw me down from a great rock, so that any other beggar may be careful not to deceive.”
sentences.n: εἰ δέ κε μὴ ἔλθῃσιν is ‘but if he should not come’ (subjunctive, epic ending -σιν); ὡς ἀγορεύω is ‘as I say’. ἐπισσεύας is the aorist participle of ἐπισεύω ‘set on, urge on’, with δμῶας ‘servants’; βαλέειν is the infinitive ‘to throw’ in the sense of a command, with ‘me’ understood, and κατὰ … πέτρης with the genitive is ‘down from a rock’. ὄφρα with the subjunctive ἀλεύεται (ἀλέομαι ‘avoid, shun’) gives the purpose, and ἠπεροπεύειν is ‘to deceive’, the verb of the noun ἠπεροπεύς ‘deceiver’; πτωχός is ‘beggar’. The bargain is stated in full: clothes and passage if Odysseus comes, death if he does not. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσεφώνεε δῖος ὑφορβός·
sentences.l: To him answering spoke the heavenly swineherd:
sentences.i: In answer the heavenly swineherd spoke to him:
sentences.n: προσεφώνεε is the imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘speak to’, with its endings uncontracted, and it is ‘spoke to’, as it is wherever the house has met it; the line is the reply-formula with a different verb from προσέφη. δῖος ὑφορβός is ‘the heavenly swineherd’: δῖος is ‘heavenly’, and ὑφορβός ‘swineherd’ (ὑπό and φέρβω ‘feed’), a second word for the swineherd beside συβώτης.

sentences.t:
ξεῖν’, οὕτω γάρ κέν μοι ἐϋκλείη τ’ ἀρετή τε
εἴη ἐπ’ ἀνθρώπους ἅμα τ’ αὐτίκα καὶ μετέπειτα,
ὅς σ’ ἐπεὶ ἐς κλισίην ἄγαγον καὶ ξείνια δῶκα,
αὖτις δὲ κτείναιμι φίλον τ’ ἀπὸ θυμὸν ἑλοίμην·
sentences.i: “Stranger, in that way I should indeed have a good name and excellence among men, both at once and hereafter, I who, after leading you to my hut and giving you the hospitality due to guests, should then kill you and take away your dear life;
sentences.n: This is sarcasm: Eumaeus says the opposite of what he means, to refuse the bargain. οὕτω γάρ is ‘so, indeed’, the γάρ confirming, and the relative ὅς in 404 spells out the ‘so’. ἐϋκλείη is ‘good fame’ (ἐύ and the root of κλέος) and ἀρετή ‘excellence’; εἴη with κεν is ‘would be’, and ἐπ’ ἀνθρώπους ‘among men’. ἅμα τ’ αὐτίκα καὶ μετέπειτα is ‘both at once and afterwards’. ὅς is relative to μοι, ‘for me who’: ἄγαγον and δῶκα are aorists, and κτείναιμι and ἑλοίμην optatives, ‘should kill’, ‘should take’. ξείνια is ‘the things due to guests’, the house wording. ἀπὸ … ἑλοίμην is tmesis for ἀφελοίμην, the middle optative of ἀφαιρέομαι ‘take away’, and φίλον θυμόν is ‘dear life’, θυμός meaning the life that leaves the body.

sentences.t: πρόφρων κεν δὴ ἔπειτα Δία Κρονίωνα λιτοίμην.
sentences.l: Ready-minded, indeed, then, Zeus, the son of Cronus, I might entreat.
sentences.i: With a ready mind, then, I should indeed pray to Zeus, the son of Cronus.
sentences.n: The sarcasm goes on: the picture is of a man who has just broken the guest-bond and is glad to pray. πρόφρων is ‘ready-minded’, the house rendering. κεν with the optative λιτοίμην is ‘I could, I should pray’; λίσσομαι is ‘entreat, pray to’, with the accusative Δία ‘Zeus’. Κρονίων is a patronymic, ‘son of Cronus’, in apposition to Δία, as the table keeps it for Ζεὺς Κρονίων.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ὥρη δόρποιο·
sentences.l: But now it is the time of supper;
sentences.i: But now it is time for supper;
sentences.n: ὥρη is ‘time, season, hour’, and δόρποιο is the epic genitive of δόρπον ‘supper’, so ‘the time of supper’. With νῦν δέ the speaker turns from the stranger’s offer to the business of the evening. The raised dot ends the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t:
τάχιστά μοι ἔνδον ἑταῖροι
εἶεν, ἵν’ ἐν κλισίῃ λαρὸν τετυκοίμεθα δόρπον.
sentences.l:
as quickly as possible for me inside companions
may be, so that in the hut a tasty supper we may prepare.”
sentences.i: May my companions be here inside as quickly as possible, so that we can prepare a tasty supper in the hut.”
sentences.n: τάχιστα is ‘as quickly as possible’, the superlative adverb, and ἔνδον ‘inside, at home’. εἶεν is the optative of εἰμί in a wish, ‘may they be’; μοι is ‘for me’. ἵνα with the optative τετυκοίμεθα, from τεύχω, in its reduplicated aorist middle, is ‘so that we may get ready’ a meal. λαρόν is ‘tasty’; its exact sense is not known, and ‘tasty’ is the traditional guess. The speech ends here, and the quotation mark closes.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἱ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον,
ἀγχίμολον δὲ σύες τε καὶ ἀνέρες ἦλθον ὑφορβοί.
sentences.l:
So they, such things to one another were saying,
and close by came the swine and the men, the swineherds.
sentences.i: So they talked in this way with one another, and close by came the swine and the men who were swineherds.
sentences.n: ὣς, the accented form, is the adverb ‘so’ (unaccented ὡς is ‘as’), and ὣς οἱ μὲν … ἀγόρευον is the narrator’s way of closing a conversation, ‘so they were speaking’; οἱ is ‘they’, and μέν is answered by the arrival that follows. The first line has the English it has where it occurs earlier. ἀγχίμολον is ‘close by’, an adverb, and σύες is the plural of σῦς ‘swine’; ἀνέρες ‘men’ (ἀνέρες for ἄνδρες) and ὑφορβοί ‘swineherds’ stand side by side: ‘the men, the swineherds’.

sentences.t:
τὰς μὲν ἄρα ἔρξαν κατὰ ἤθεα κοιμηθῆναι,
κλαγγὴ δ’ ἄσπετος ὦρτο συῶν αὐλιζομενάων
αὐτὰρ ὁ οἷς ἑτάροισιν ἐκέκλετο δῖος ὑφορβός·
sentences.i: They shut the swine up to sleep in their usual places, and a boundless clamour rose from the swine as they settled in for the night. Then the heavenly swineherd gave orders to his own companions:
sentences.n: τάς is ‘them’, the swine: σῦς can be feminine, and so can the pronoun. ἔρξαν is the aorist of ἔργω ‘shut in, pen’, and κατὰ ἤθεα is ‘in their accustomed places’ (ἦθος, plural ἤθεα); κοιμηθῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive with an active sense, ‘to go to sleep’. κλαγγή is ‘clamour’, ἄσπετος ‘boundless’ (literally ‘not to be told’), and ὦρτο the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘arise’, with συῶν αὐλιζομενάων ‘of the swine bedding down in the yard’. The source prints no stop at the end of 412, so the unit runs on to 413. ὁ is the pronoun ‘he’, with δῖος ὑφορβός in apposition; οἷς is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative; ἐκέκλετο is the reduplicated aorist middle of κέλομαι ‘call to, order’, ‘gave orders to’.

sentences.t:
ἄξεθ’ ὑῶν τὸν ἄριστον, ἵνα ξείνῳ ἱερεύσω
τηλεδαπῷ·
sentences.l:
“Bring the best of the swine, so that for a stranger I may slaughter,
from-a-far-land;
sentences.i: “Bring the best of the swine, so that I may slaughter it for the stranger from a far-off land;
sentences.n: ἄξεθ’ is ἄξετε, the aorist imperative of ἄγω ‘bring’, with the final consonant changed before the aspirate that follows; ὑῶν is the genitive plural of ὗς ‘swine’, a partitive, ‘of the swine’, and ἄριστον is ‘best’. ἵνα with the subjunctive ἱερεύσω is ‘so that I may slaughter’: ἱερεύω is the verb for killing a beast for sacrifice, and here it is the killing for a meal. ξείνῳ τηλεδαπῷ is ‘to the stranger from far off’ (from τῆλε ‘far’), dative of the one the animal is killed for. The raised dot ends the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t:
πρὸς δ’ αὐτοὶ ὀνησόμεθ’, οἵ περ ὀϊζὺν
δὴν ἔχομεν πάσχοντες ὑῶν ἕνεκ’ ἀργιοδόντων·
sentences.l:
and besides, ourselves we shall have enjoyment, we who distress
for long have, suffering, because of the white-toothed pigs;
sentences.i: and besides, we ourselves shall have our enjoyment of it, we who have long been beset by distress, suffering for the sake of the white-toothed pigs;
sentences.n: πρὸς δέ is ‘and besides’, πρός being an adverb here; ὀνησόμεθ’ is the future middle of ὀνίνημι ‘profit, have benefit’, and the meal is the thing enjoyed. οἵ περ is ‘we who indeed’. ὀϊζύς is ‘distress’, ὀϊζυρός ‘sorrowful’ being its adjective; ἔχομεν πάσχοντες is literally ‘we have, suffering’, and with δήν ‘for long’ it is ‘we have long been suffering’. ὑῶν ἕνεκ’ ἀργιοδόντων is ‘for the sake of the white-toothed pigs’: ἀργιόδοντες is ἀργός ‘white’ with ὀδούς ‘tooth’, the epithet of pigs.

sentences.t: ἄλλοι δ’ ἡμέτερον κάματον νήποινον ἔδουσιν.
sentences.l: but others our toil, unpunished, devour.”
sentences.i: while others devour what we have toiled for and pay nothing for it.”
sentences.n: ἄλλοι is ‘others’, the suitors, not named. κάματος, ‘weariness’ elsewhere in the house, is here the toil and what comes of it, so ‘our toil’ and in English ‘what we have toiled for’. νήποινον is the word of 377, ‘unpunished, unpaid for’, and ἔδουσιν ‘they eat, devour’; the line is the answer to the swineherds’ own hardship in 415–416, and it repeats Eumaeus’s grievance of 375–377. The speech ends here, and the quotation mark closes.
